questions.stem: Which of the following is not an element of weather and climate?
explanation_steps: The textbook: weather and climate are the study of the conditions of air temperature, air pressure, wind and precipitation (plus humidity) – these are the ELEMENTS.
Latitude is a FACTOR (control) that influences climate, together with altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents and relief.
Answer: D.
tips: Elements = what we measure (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, precipitation). Factors = what causes differences (latitude, altitude, distance from sea…).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a factor (control) of climate rather than an element?
explanation_steps: Humidity, rainfall, wind and temperature are measured elements.
Altitude influences temperature – a factor. Answer: C.

questions.stem: An expansive population pyramid:

options.B: has a large number of people of younger ages
options.C: is commonly used for developing countries

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Expansive: a pyramid showing rapid population growth with larger number of people of younger age.'
It adds that developing countries are represented best by expansive pyramids, while most developed countries have constrictive and stationary types.
All of A–C are correct. Answer: D.
tips: Expansive = wide base (many children) → rapid growth → developing countries. Constrictive = narrow base → slow growth. Stationary = near-zero growth.

similar_questions.stem: A population pyramid with a narrow base and roughly equal numbers in all age groups indicates:
explanation_steps: Equal numbers of all ages → stationary pyramid → near zero growth.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.4 Population Growth and Structure – types of population pyramid

questions.stem: People who have lived in a place for many generations live in a/an:
explanation_steps: Textbook classification by permanence: ephemeral (1–7 days), temporary (1–30 days), seasonal (several months), semi-permanent (several years), permanent (several generations).
Answer: B.
tips: Learn the five time spans in order: days → weeks → months → years → generations.

similar_questions.stem: A herders' camp that lasts for several months in one place is a:
explanation_steps: Several months = seasonal settlement.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The reasons why Eritrea shows a wide variety of wildlife are:
explanation_steps: The textbook: Eritrea has a varied relief and climate, therefore it has varied natural vegetation and wildlife.
It also notes that the different vegetation types (acacia grassland, mountain vegetation, halophytic desert vegetation, mangroves) 'attract different kinds of animals'.
Altitude (relief), climate and vegetation all contribute. Answer: E.
tips: Chain: relief/altitude → climate → vegetation → wildlife.

similar_questions.stem: Why do the vegetation belts of the eastern escarpment change from acacia at the foot to olive and juniper higher up?
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'This vertical distribution of the trees is determined by temperature.'
Temperature falls with altitude. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Natural Vegetation and Wildlife in Eritrea

additional_textbook_refs.unit: Unit 4 – Natural Vegetation and Wildlife in Eritrea
additional_textbook_refs.section: 4.6.2 Present Situation of Wildlife in Eritrea

questions.stem: The latest ethnic group to migrate to Eritrea is the:
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 7.1: Afar, Saho, Bilen and Hidarb belong to the Hamitic (Kushitic) family; the Rashaida belong to the Semitic family.
The textbook calls the Semitic families (from the Arabian Peninsula) the latest migrants; the Rashaida, who live in the Northern Red Sea region, came from Arabia most recently (in the 19th century).
Answer: A.
tips: Order of arrival in the textbook: Pygmoid (earliest) → Nilotic → Hamitic (Kushitic) → Semitic (latest).

similar_questions.stem: Which Eritrean ethnic group belongs to the Nilotic family?
explanation_steps: Table 7.1: Nilotic – Nara and Kunama.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: The textbook calls the Semites the latest migrants; the Rashaida's 19th-century arrival is general knowledge.

questions.stem: Which of the following equipment was not produced by local artisans in cottage industries?
explanation_steps: The textbook: before modern industries, local artisans in cottage industries made ploughs, sickles, knives, axes, clothes, bags and pots.
A video camera is a modern electronic product of large-scale industry. Answer: C.
tips: Cottage industry = small, traditional, home-based production with simple tools and local materials.

similar_questions.stem: Traditional cottage industries in Eritrea mainly use:

options.B: simple tools and local raw materials

explanation_steps: Artisans make ploughs, pots, baskets and cloth by hand from local materials.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Odd one out from the following alternatives:
explanation_steps: Faulting, folding, earthquakes and volcanism are TECTONIC (internal) forces (G11 Unit 1).
Running water is a GRADATIONAL (external) agent that wears down and builds up the land (G11 Unit 2).
Answer: D.
tips: Internal (tectonic) forces build relief; external (gradational) agents – running water, wind, waves, ice – level it.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these is a gradational agent?
explanation_steps: Only wind acts on the surface to erode and deposit.
Answer: C.

additional_textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Gradation by Rivers and Winds

questions.stem: From a temperature graph, several pieces of information can be obtained, such as:

options.A: hotness and coldness of a place
options.B: whether the climate is hot or cold

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'We can use the graph to describe … whether the temperature is high or low throughout the year … how the temperature varies within a year … whether the climate is hot or cold.'
So A and B are clearly correct. Option C is incomplete ('Factors that determine') and the textbook does not say a graph shows the factors.
No option says 'A and B'. The setter most likely intended E (All of the above); key E with low confidence.
tips: A temperature line graph: months on the horizontal axis, °C on the vertical axis; it shows level, variation and the annual range of temperature.

similar_questions.stem: On a temperature line graph, the months of the year are shown on the:
explanation_steps: The textbook: temperature in °C on the vertical line, months on the horizontal line.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.4 Air Temperature – graphic representation of temperature

questions.review_flag: No option matches the textbook exactly: A and B are both correct, C is incomplete ('Factors that determine') and there is no 'A and B' option. Key E; A and B accepted – teacher decision.

questions.stem: The type of climate with the lowest annual temperatures in the world is:
explanation_steps: The textbook: polar climates 'are known for their permanently cold conditions. No month has an average temperature of more than 10 °C. They have the lowest annual temperatures in the world.'
Answer: C.
tips: Polar climates: farthest from the equator, inadequate sunlight – tundra and ice-cap types.

similar_questions.stem: In polar climates, no month has an average temperature above:
explanation_steps: The textbook gives 10 °C.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Major Types of World Climates

questions.stem: The division of soil into sandy loam, loam and silty clay is based on:
explanation_steps: The textbook: soil texture refers to the size of soil particles – sand, silt and clay.
Names such as sandy loam, loam and silty clay are texture classes that describe the proportions of sand, silt and clay.
Answer: A.
tips: Texture = particle size (sand > silt > clay). Structure = how particles are grouped. Profile = vertical layers.

similar_questions.stem: Which soil particle is the smallest?
explanation_steps: Clay particles are too small to be seen by the naked eye (textbook).
Answer: D.

questions.stem: The largest island in Eritrea is:
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The largest island is called Dahlak Kebir (Table 6.2).' Nora (Norah), north of Dahlak Kebir, is the second largest.
Answer: C.
tips: Dahlak Kebir is also a historical site (early Islamic period).

similar_questions.stem: The second largest island of Eritrea is:
explanation_steps: The textbook: the Nora island north of Dahlak Kebir is the second largest.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 6 – Strategic Position, Size and Shape of Eritrea
textbook_ref.section: 6.3 The Size and Shape of Eritrea – islands (Table 6.2)

questions.stem: Industrial and political regions are examples of:
explanation_steps: The textbook distinguishes physical regions (based on natural features – soil, climate, landforms) from cultural regions (based on human or cultural features).

Language regions are single-feature cultural regions and economic regions are multiple-feature cultural regions; industrial (economic) and political regions are defined by human activities – cultural regions.
Answer: A.
tips: Physical/natural regions: climate, soil, landform, vegetation. Cultural regions: language, religion, political, economic/industrial.

similar_questions.stem: A soil region and a climate region are examples of:
explanation_steps: Both are defined by natural features.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 4.1–4.2 Place Similarity and Regions; The Concept of Regions – physical and cultural regions

questions.stem: Settlements found close to sources of water supply are:
explanation_steps: The textbook: settlements that develop near springs, wells, rivers and lakes are called wet-point settlements; besides drinking water they provide water for animals and crops.
Answer: B.
tips: Wet-point = near water (dry regions). Dry-point = on raised ground away from flooding (wet regions).

similar_questions.stem: A village built on a small hill to escape seasonal floods is a:
explanation_steps: Raised, flood-free sites give dry-point settlements.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 4.2.1 Basic factors that determine the site of rural settlements

questions.stem: Tropical climate is more influenced by ______ than by any other factor.
explanation_steps: The textbook (tropical climates, within 20° of the equator): 'This type of climate is influenced more by latitudinal location than any other factor.'
The sun is high in the sky every day, giving high temperatures all year. Answer: C.
tips: Low latitude → high sun angle → high temperatures throughout the year.

similar_questions.stem: Tropical climates are found approximately within:
explanation_steps: The textbook: the tropical climate is found within 20° of the equator in both hemispheres.
Answer: A.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Major Types of World Climates

questions.stem: The speed of wind is measured by:
explanation_steps: The textbook: wind speed is measured by an anemometer; the most common is the three-cup anemometer.
A barometer measures air pressure, a hygrometer humidity, a rain gauge rainfall and a wind vane wind DIRECTION.
Answer: E.
tips: Wind vane → direction; anemometer → speed.

similar_questions.stem: Which instrument shows the direction from which the wind blows?
explanation_steps: The wind vane points into the wind.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.6 Winds and Wind Belts – measuring wind speed

questions.stem: During which colonial rule did Eritrea's economy substantially transform?
explanation_steps: The textbook: during the Italian colonial period (1890–1941) the Italians built factories (their number grew rapidly), roads, railways and ports; in the 1940s–50s Eritrea had a highly developed industrial base by African colonial standards – 'a radical transformation in terms of urbanization and industrialization'.
The British weakened the economy and the industrial sector declined after Ethiopia's occupation.
Answer: C.
tips: Modern industry and modern transport both began in Eritrea during the Italian period.

similar_questions.stem: Modern transport (roads linking the ports with the hinterland) began in Eritrea during the:
explanation_steps: The textbook: modern transport began during the Italian colonial period.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Alcohol freezes at:
explanation_steps: The textbook (minimum thermometer): mercury cannot be used at very low temperatures because it freezes at −40 °C, while some places reach about −87 °C; 'Alcohol freezes at −130 °C'.
Answer: B (textbook value).
tips: Minimum thermometer uses alcohol (low freezing point); maximum thermometer uses mercury.
Scientific values: ethanol freezes at about −114 °C and mercury at about −39 °C – the textbook rounds these; answer with the textbook values in the exam.

similar_questions.stem: Why is mercury NOT used in a minimum thermometer in very cold regions?
explanation_steps: The textbook: mercury freezes at −40 °C, but temperatures can fall to about −87 °C.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.4 Air Temperature – maximum and minimum thermometers

questions.review_flag: Superscript degree signs lost in the text version ('-1300C' = −130 °C). The textbook's −130 °C differs from the scientific value for ethanol (≈ −114 °C); key follows the textbook.

questions.stem: If we say 'Sawa is very hot', this refers to:
explanation_steps: The textbook: weather is the condition of the atmosphere over a SHORT period (part of a day, a day, a week, a season); climate is the average condition over a long period.
'Sawa is very hot' has no time reference – it describes Sawa's usual (long-term) condition, i.e. its climate. ('Today Sawa is very hot' would be weather.)
Answer: C.
tips: Look for time words: 'today/yesterday/this week' → weather; general or 'usually/every year' → climate.

similar_questions.stem: 'Yesterday it was cloudy and windy in Asmara' describes:
explanation_steps: A specific short time (yesterday) → weather.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1–3.2 The Atmosphere; Relationship between Weather and Climate

questions.review_flag: Ambiguous: without a time reference the statement is taken as climate (C); some teachers may key A (weather). Teacher decision.

questions.stem: In the ______ continent, the discovery of new agricultural land caused a relative increase in world population growth between 1000 and 1650 AD.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The discovery of new agricultural land in America, Australia and Africa, as well as the growth of commerce … caused a relative increase of the world population. Between 1000 and 1650 …'
Of the options, Africa is named directly; Australia (part of Oceania) is also named, so C is defensible.
Key B (Africa); C also accepted.
tips: Slow growth before the industrial revolution: high infant mortality, short life expectancy, famines and undernourishment.

similar_questions.stem: Up to the industrial revolution the world population grew slowly mainly because of:

options.B: high infant mortality, short life expectancy and famines

explanation_steps: The textbook lists high infant mortality, short life expectancy, periodic famines and undernourishment.
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: The textbook names America, Australia and Africa: both Africa (B) and Oceania/Australia (C) are in the options. Key B, C accepted.

questions.stem: Migration of people into or out of a country can change:
explanation_steps: The textbook: migration affects the area of out-migration, the area of in-migration and the migrants; it changes the demographic structure (number, density, growth, age, sex).
It may increase a region's burden on resources or its capacity to exploit resources (economic development), and migrants carry their culture with them.
Answer: E.
tips: Migration effects: demographic (numbers, density, age, sex), economic (labour, remittances), social/cultural.

similar_questions.stem: Net migration rate = (immigrants − emigrants) ÷ mid-year population × 1000. If immigrants = 40,000, emigrants = 20,000 and population = 9,000,000, the rate is about:
explanation_steps: Answer: A.

questions.stem: The highest peak in the Central Plateau is:
explanation_steps: The textbook: in the Central (Hamasien) Plateau, 'Emba Tekera, 2579 m above sea level, is the highest peak.'
Emba Soira (3013 m) is in the Eastern Highlands, Hager Nues in the Northern Highlands, Mt Ghini in the Upper Anseba Highlands and Emba Tekillo in the Mereb Trough.
Answer: B.
tips: Match each peak to its region: Soira – Eastern Highlands; Hager Nues – Northern; Ghini – Upper Anseba; Tekera – Central Plateau.

similar_questions.stem: The highest peak in Eritrea is:
explanation_steps: Table 7.1: Emba Soira, 3013 m, Eastern Highlands.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 7 – Relief and Drainage Systems in Eritrea
textbook_ref.section: 7.1.3 The Highlands – c) The Central Plateau

questions.stem: Soil erosion can be controlled by all of the following except:

options.A: ploughing up and down the slope

explanation_steps: The textbook's soil conservation measures: terracing, contour ploughing, shelter belts, check dams and reforestation; overgrazing must be avoided.
Ploughing UP AND DOWN a slope makes furrows that channel runoff downhill and increases erosion – contour ploughing (across the slope) is the conservation method.
Answer: A.
tips: Plough ACROSS the slope (along the contour), never up and down.

similar_questions.stem: Ploughing along the contour reduces erosion because:

options.B: the furrows trap water and slow runoff

explanation_steps: Contour furrows act as small barriers that hold water and let it infiltrate.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: In which period did the Horn of Africa begin to sink and the Indian Ocean invade the land?
explanation_steps: The textbook (Mesozoic Era): 'During the early stage of the Mesozoic era, i.e. the Triassic Period, the Horn of Africa began to sink gradually. As a result, the Indian Ocean invaded the land from southeast to northwest.'
The invasion continued until the Jurassic, when the sea reached its northern limit (Halay–Digsa–Gurae–Mendefera line).
Answer: D.
tips: Mesozoic periods in order: Triassic → Jurassic → Cretaceous. Sinking began in the Triassic; the sea reached its limit in the Jurassic.

similar_questions.stem: The advancing Mesozoic sea reached its northern limit in Eritrea along the Halay–Digsa–Gurae–Mendefera line during the:
explanation_steps: The textbook: it reached this northern limit in the Jurassic Period.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: When the splitting continued, Laurasia was broken into:
explanation_steps: The textbook: Pangaea first split into Gondwanaland and Laurasia; 'in the northern hemisphere Laurasia split into North America and Eurasia (Europe and Asia)'.
Africa, South America, India and Australia/New Zealand came from Gondwanaland.
Answer: D.
tips: Laurasia (north) → North America + Eurasia. Gondwanaland (south) → South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica.

similar_questions.stem: Which landmass was part of Gondwanaland?
explanation_steps: South America was in the southern supercontinent.
Answer: D.

questions.stem: The local time difference between 105°E and 180°E is:
explanation_steps: Both places are east of Greenwich, so subtract: 180° − 105° = 75° of longitude.
The textbook: places 15° apart in longitude have a one-hour time difference.
75° ÷ 15° = 5 hours. Answer: A.
tips: Same hemisphere (both E or both W) → subtract; opposite sides of the prime meridian → add.
1° = 4 minutes; 15° = 1 hour.

similar_questions.stem: When it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich (0°), what is the local time at 45°E?
explanation_steps: 45° ÷ 15° = 3 hours; east of Greenwich time is ahead.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2 Rotation of the Earth and its Effects – differences in local time

questions.review_flag: Degree signs lost in the text version ('1050 E and1800 E' = 105°E and 180°E).

questions.stem: The type of natural vegetation found in the upper part of the Eastern Escarpment is:
explanation_steps: The textbook: from the coast to the foot of the escarpment there are short umbrella-shaped acacias; 'Along the eastern Escarpment, there are olive trees and Juniper'; on the plateau, euphorbia and junipers.
Mangroves grow on the coast and islands; succulents and xerophytes in dry lowlands; savannah in the western lowlands.
Answer: B.
tips: Vertical zoning of vegetation is controlled by temperature (altitude).

similar_questions.stem: Mangrove forests in Eritrea are found:

options.B: along the coast and on the islands

explanation_steps: The textbook: mangrove forests thrive in the coastal areas and islands.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Natural Vegetation and Wildlife in Eritrea

questions.stem: One of the following is an example of a historical site of tourist attraction:
explanation_steps: The textbook (Tourism): 'The historical sites of the country include those located at Adulis, Cohaito, Keskese, Tekhond'e, Metera and Der'at.'
Volcanic landscapes, the coastal plain, the Green Belt and the escarpment are NATURAL attractions.
Answer: D.
tips: Historical/archaeological: Adulis, Cohaito, Metera, Keskese; Italian-period buildings of Asmara; Massawa and Dahlak Kebir (Islamic/Turkish).

similar_questions.stem: Which is a natural (not historical) tourist attraction?
explanation_steps: The Green Belt forest is a natural feature.
Answer: D.

questions.stem: The movement of the earth on its axis which takes 24 hours is called:
explanation_steps: The textbook: the rotation of the earth on its axis, completed in about 24 hours, 'is known as the daily motion of the earth'. It causes day and night.
The annual motion (revolution) around the sun takes 365¼ days.
Answer: C.
tips: Rotation = daily motion (24 h) → day/night, local time, deflection of winds, tides. Revolution = annual motion → seasons.

similar_questions.stem: The revolution of the earth around the sun takes about:
explanation_steps: Annual motion = 365¼ days.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2 Rotation of the Earth and its Effects

questions.stem: In a remote area in 2015 the number of births and deaths were 100 and 50 respectively. If the total mid-year population was 2000, find the birth and death rates.
explanation_steps: Textbook formula: birth rate = total number of births ÷ mid-year population × 1000 (per thousand).
Answer: E (50 and 25).
tips: Crude rates are per 1000 people. Natural increase = (BR − DR) ÷ 10 % = (50 − 25) ÷ 10 = 2.5 %.

similar_questions.stem: A town of 40,000 people had 1,200 births and 400 deaths in a year. What is the natural increase rate in percent?

textbook_ref.section: 3.4 Population Growth and Structure – birth and death rates

questions.stem: A confluence is a point where:
explanation_steps: The textbook: the place where two rivers or streams meet is called a confluence.
Where a river begins is its source (headwater); where it enters the sea is its mouth.
Answer: C.
tips: Source → tributaries join at confluences → mouth (delta or estuary).

similar_questions.stem: Khartoum is located at the confluence of:

options.B: the Blue Nile and the White Nile

explanation_steps: The textbook (settlement sites): Khartoum is at the confluence of the Blue Nile and the White Nile.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Gradation by Rivers and Winds

questions.stem: Which of the following combinations is not correctly matched?
explanation_steps: Isotherms join places with the same temperature (textbook), not pressure.
Isohyets – equal rainfall; hygrometer – humidity; isobars – equal pressure; anemometer – wind speed – all correct.
Answer: A.
tips: Iso-therm (heat), iso-bar (pressure), iso-hyet (rain).

similar_questions.stem: Lines joining places of equal atmospheric pressure are:
explanation_steps: Equal pressure = isobars.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following are the main areas of volcanoes and earthquakes?

options.A: West coast of North and South America

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The main areas of volcanoes and earthquakes are the Pacific ring of fire, the Alpine-Himalayan Belt, and the Mid-Atlantic Oceanic Ridge.'
The west coast of North and South America is part of the Pacific Ring of Fire.
Answer: E.
tips: Volcanoes and earthquakes occur along plate boundaries.

similar_questions.stem: Why are volcanoes and earthquakes common around the Pacific Ocean?

options.B: Because plates meet along its margins

explanation_steps: The Pacific Ring of Fire follows convergent plate boundaries (subduction zones).
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The geological era to which the formation of fossil soils belongs is the:
explanation_steps: The textbook (Palaeozoic Era, 225–600 million years ago): the surface was heavily weathered, forming peneplains; the weathered soils were preserved by overlying rocks – 'These preserved soils are called fossil soils.'
They are made of iron and kaolin (reddish) and outcrop around Asmara.
Answer: C.
tips: Eras of Eritrea's geology: Precambrian (crystalline rocks) → Palaeozoic (fossil soils) → Mesozoic (marine sediments) → Cenozoic (basalts, rift, sediments).

similar_questions.stem: The fossil soils around Asmara are reddish because they contain:
explanation_steps: The textbook: they are made of iron and kaolin which give them their reddish colour.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The altitude of Eritrea ranges from 3013 m above sea level at Emba Soira to 100 m below sea level in the Danakil Depression. So the range of altitude is:
explanation_steps: One height is above and the other below sea level, so ADD them: 3013 + 100 = 3113 m.
Answer: A (using the figures given in the question).
tips: Range between + and − heights = sum of the two numbers.
Note: the Grade 11 textbook gives about 116 m below sea level for the Danakil Depression, which would give 3129 m (option D).

similar_questions.stem: A mountain is 2400 m above sea level and a nearby depression 75 m below sea level. What is the difference in height?
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 7 – Relief and Drainage Systems in Eritrea

questions.review_flag: Stem gives −100 m for the Danakil Depression; the textbook gives about −116 m, which would make option D (3129 m) correct. Key A follows the data in the stem.

questions.stem: Coarse-textured soils are the result of:
explanation_steps: The textbook (soils in Eritrea): 'Due to slow weathering, these soils are coarse in texture' – e.g. shallow, coarse soils of the lowlands where rainfall is low and chemical weathering slow.
Intense weathering breaks rocks into fine particles (clays).
Answer: C.
tips: Slow weathering → large particles → coarse, shallow soils. Intense weathering → fine, deep soils.

similar_questions.stem: Why are soils in the Eritrean lowlands generally shallow and coarse?

options.B: Because low rainfall makes weathering slow

explanation_steps: In dry lowlands chemical weathering is slow, so soils stay shallow and coarse.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All are minor features produced by wave erosion during the process of cliff formation except:
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Caves, Blowholes, Arches, and Stacks: These are minor features' formed as waves attack a cliff (cave → blowhole → arch → stack).
Bays (with headlands) are larger features formed where soft rock along a coast is eroded more quickly – not one of the minor cliff features.
Answer: D.
tips: Sequence: crack → cave → blowhole (hole in the roof) → arch (cave cut through a headland) → stack (arch roof collapses) → stump.

similar_questions.stem: When the roof of a sea arch collapses, the isolated pillar of rock left standing is a:
explanation_steps: Collapse of an arch leaves a stack.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Gradation by the Action of Waves

questions.stem: A type of settlement that develops where a minor road joins a major road is:
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'There are other forms, like the T-shaped, which develop at a place where a minor road joins a major road.'
Star-shaped settlements spread along several major roads; radial forms converge on a central nucleus; linear forms follow one street, river or coast.
Answer: E.
tips: Shape follows the attracting feature: one road/river → linear; crossroads of many roads → star; minor meets major road → T-shaped.

similar_questions.stem: Houses arranged closely in a circle around an open central space (e.g. kraals) form a:
explanation_steps: The textbook: rounded settlements – houses in a circular form around an open space; kraals of sub-Saharan Africa.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Surveyed features (points fixed by survey) are represented on maps by:
explanation_steps: The textbook: trigonometrical stations 'are points on the earth's surface that are used for triangulation survey'; they are shown by small triangles with the altitude and are more accurate than spot heights.
Hachures, hill shading, form lines and physiographic diagrams are pictorial methods of showing relief that are not based on exact surveyed heights (form lines are 'approximate contours').
Answer: D.
tips: Accurate height methods: spot heights, trigonometrical stations, bench marks, contours. Pictorial: hachures, hill shading, form lines, physiographic diagrams.

similar_questions.stem: A mark engraved on a building or bridge showing its exact height above mean sea level is a:
explanation_steps: The textbook: bench marks are marks on buildings, bridges or pillars, shown as B.M. with the height.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 5 – The Representation of Relief on Maps
textbook_ref.section: 5.1.6 Others – spot heights, trigonometrical stations, bench marks

questions.review_flag: Ungrammatical stem ('Survey of features is represented on maps by'); interpreted as 'features fixed by survey'.

questions.stem: African countries are categorised as underdeveloped, except:
explanation_steps: The textbook (economic measures of development) singles out the Republic of South Africa: in sub-Saharan African countries, 'excluding the Republic of South Africa', more than 60 % of the population works in agriculture.
South Africa is the most industrialised economy in Africa; Uganda, Angola, Egypt and Tunisia are developing countries.

similar_questions.stem: In the least developed countries such as Eritrea, Ethiopia and Chad, what share of the population is engaged in agriculture (textbook)?

explanation_steps: Textbook method: daily average temperature = (maximum + minimum) ÷ 2.
Answer: B. (20.5 °C is the daily RANGE; 64.1 °C is just the sum.)
tips: Daily range = max − min; daily mean = (max + min) ÷ 2.

similar_questions.stem: Massawa's highest monthly mean is 34.8 °C (July) and the lowest 25.6 °C (January). What is the annual range?
explanation_steps: Annual range = highest − lowest monthly mean = 34.8 − 25.6 = 9.2 °C.

similar_questions.stem: Roads, piped water, sewerage and electricity lines are examples of a settlement's:
explanation_steps: These are networks – infrastructure.

similar_questions.stem: In Eritrea, elephants are found mainly around:

questions.stem: Aged plastic materials that are not discarded as waste but used again are an example of ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook: in recycling, resources are used over and over again – 'old items like aged cars are not discarded as waste but are taken back to factories where they are smelted' and reused.
Substitution replaces a scarce resource with another (e.g. plastic for metals, solar for oil).
Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Replacing oil with solar or wind energy is an example of:

questions.stem: The winter season in the southern hemisphere begins in:

Winter in the southern hemisphere begins at the June solstice (21 June), when the overhead sun is over the Tropic of Cancer.
Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: On 21/22 December the overhead sun is over the:

questions.stem: One of the following is false about cultural impact on the natural environment:

options.A: Modern technology always has a positive impact on the environment.
options.B: Today desertification is taking place at a much faster rate than in the past.
options.C: Many environmental problems have become global in nature.
options.D: Global warming is causing the melting of global ice or snow.
options.E: Acid rain is produced by a large volume of pollutants in the atmosphere.

explanation_steps: The textbook: modern technology enables people to modify the environment but also produces hazardous by-products and pollution – its impact is NOT always positive.

B, C and E agree with Unit 5: environmental degradation (deforestation) is faster than in the past, problems such as global warming and acid rain are global, and acid rain is 'the product of a large volume of pollutants into the atmosphere'. D (melting of ice) is not in the textbook's list of consequences of global warming, but it is true.
Answer: A.
tips: Words like 'always' or 'never' often signal a false statement.

similar_questions.stem: According to the textbook, which is a consequence of global warming?

options.B: A rise in sea level that may flood coastal lands

explanation_steps: The textbook lists a rise in sea level, disruption of agriculture by frequent droughts, and depletion of the ozone layer.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The lapse rate of temperature can be defined as:

options.A: increase of temperature as altitude increases
options.B: decrease of temperature as altitude decreases
options.C: increase of temperature as altitude decreases
options.D: increase in density of air upward with altitude
options.E: decrease in density of air downward with altitude

explanation_steps: The textbook: temperature decreases by 6.5 °C for every 1000 m increase in altitude; 'this rate of decrease of temperature with increase in altitude is called lapse rate of temperature'.
The same relationship read in the other direction is 'temperature increases as altitude decreases' – option C. A and B reverse the relationship; D and E are about air density, not temperature.
Answer: C.
tips: Normal lapse rate = 6.5 °C per 1000 m (0.65 °C per 100 m).

similar_questions.stem: If the temperature at sea level is 30 °C, what is the temperature at 2000 m (normal lapse rate)?
explanation_steps: 30 − 13 = 17 °C. Answer: A.

questions.review_flag: The expected definition (decrease of temperature with increasing altitude) is only given in reversed form (option C).

questions.stem: Water resource development in the Eritrean Highlands is hindered by:
explanation_steps: The textbook lists the major water problems of the Eritrean Highlands: (a) groundwater is easily depleted due to heavy pumping for irrigation; (b) siltation is a serious problem in surface water development.
Low recharge rate is given as a problem of the lowland zones (e.g. western lowlands), not the Highlands (recharge 50–150 mm/year there).
Answer: E (C and D).
tips: Highlands: over-pumping + siltation. Lowlands: meagre rainfall, low recharge, salinity, high evapo-transpiration.

similar_questions.stem: Which water development methods does the textbook recommend for the Highlands?

options.B: Dug wells, boreholes, river diversion, small dams and roof-water cisterns
options.E: Nothing – no water can be developed

explanation_steps: The textbook: dug wells, boreholes, river diversion, small-scale dams and cisterns.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Most summer rainfall in Eritrea is:
explanation_steps: The Grade 12 textbook explains that summer rain comes when the ITCZ moves north of Eritrea and moist south-westerly winds from the Gulf of Guinea and Zaire Basin cross the country; it does not name the rainfall type.
Relief (A) and orographic (D) are the same thing, as are cyclonic (C) and frontal (E) (Grade 9 textbook), so none of these pairs can be the single best answer.

Summer rain in Eritrea mostly falls as afternoon thunderstorms from strong heating and rising moist air – convectional rainfall (textbook: heavy rain with thunderstorms and lightning in the late afternoon). Key: B.
tips: Rainfall types (G9): convectional (heating), frontal/cyclonic (air masses meet), relief/orographic (mountain barrier; rain shadow on the leeward side).

similar_questions.stem: Rainfall caused when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier is:
explanation_steps: Mountain barriers force air up → relief/orographic rainfall; the leeward side is the rain shadow.
Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Textbook does not name the type of Eritrea's summer rain. A and D are synonyms (as are C and E), so B is chosen by elimination and standard climatology; teacher should confirm.

questions.stem: The process by which rain water dissolves minerals in rocks is called:
explanation_steps: The textbook (chemical weathering): 'When rain water dissolves minerals in rocks, this process is called solution.'
Hydration is absorption of water causing expansion; oxidation is reaction with oxygen (rusting); carbonation is reaction with carbonic acid; exfoliation is physical peeling of rock layers.
Answer: A.
tips: Solution dissolves rock salt; carbonation attacks limestone.

similar_questions.stem: Minerals that absorb water, increase in volume and cause rocks to break up undergo:
explanation_steps: The textbook describes this as absorption of water (hydration).
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Ato Ahmed has planted lines of trees across his flat farmland in order to prevent:
explanation_steps: Lines of trees across open flat land are shelter belts (windbreaks) – one of the textbook's soil conservation measures.
They reduce wind speed near the ground and so reduce wind erosion. Flat land is not threatened by waves or rivers in this sense.
Answer: B.
tips: Shelter belts → wind erosion; terraces/contour ploughing/check dams → water erosion.

similar_questions.stem: Check dams built across a gully mainly reduce:
explanation_steps: Check dams slow runoff and trap sediment in gullies.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Winds that blow from the slowly rotating poles towards the fast-rotating equator are deflected towards the:
explanation_steps: The textbook (Coriolis effect): in the northern hemisphere winds are deflected to the RIGHT and in the southern hemisphere to the LEFT.

A wind moving south towards the equator in the northern hemisphere turns right → towards the west; a wind moving north towards the equator in the southern hemisphere turns left → also towards the west.
The ground under the wind moves eastward faster near the equator, so the wind lags behind, i.e. towards the west. Answer: C (hence the polar EASTERLIES and trade winds blow from the east).
tips: Winds are named from where they come: a wind deflected towards the west is an easterly wind.

similar_questions.stem: Winds blowing from the equator towards the poles in the northern hemisphere are deflected towards the:
explanation_steps: Moving north and turning right → towards the east (westerlies).
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2 Rotation of the Earth and its Effects – deflection of winds

questions.stem: Identify one of the following that is an effect of the earth's rotation:

options.A: change in the length of day and night

explanation_steps: The textbook's effects of rotation: day and night, apparent movement of the sun (east to west), differences in local time, deflection of winds, tides.
Changes in the length of day and night, change of seasons and the calendar year result from the REVOLUTION of the earth (with its tilted axis).
Answer: B.
tips: Rotation → day/night, sun's apparent daily path, local time, Coriolis, tides. Revolution → seasons, varying day length, calendar year.

similar_questions.stem: Which is an effect of the earth's revolution?

options.B: Apparent daily movement of the sun

explanation_steps: Only the seasons come from revolution (with axial tilt).
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following roads is asphalt?
explanation_steps: The textbook lists roads built in the Italian period: Mendefera–Areza (37 km), Dekemhare–Tsorona (66 km), Dekemhare–Teraemni and Dekemhare–Nefasit (40 km), and all-weather roads built after independence (Keren–Afabet, Dekemhare–Tserona, Mendefera–Barentu–Tessenei).
The textbook never says which roads are asphalt. Dekemhare–Nefasit is a long-established paved road; the key follows local knowledge only.
Key: C (low confidence).
tips: The textbook classifies roads as primary, secondary and feeder roads; 'all-weather road' does not necessarily mean asphalt.

options.A: link the ports with the hinterland

explanation_steps: The textbook: Italian roads aimed to link the ports with the hinterland, develop agriculture, exploit minerals and carry freight.
Answer: A.

questions.stem: Tropical rainforests are characterised by the following features except:

options.C: sunshine is prevented from reaching the ground
options.E: support a variety of wild animals

explanation_steps: The textbook's features of tropical wet (rainforest) vegetation: broad-leaved evergreen trees, tall hardwood trees forming a canopy that prevents sunshine reaching the ground, and 'the dense vegetation supports a great variety of wild animals'.
Deciduous, scattered trees describe savannah/monsoon or temperate deciduous forests, not rainforest.
Answer: D.
tips: Rainforest: dense, evergreen, layered canopy. Savannah: grass with scattered trees. Temperate deciduous: trees shed leaves in winter.

similar_questions.stem: The largest areas of tropical wet climate and rainforest are found in:
explanation_steps: The textbook: upper Amazon basin, western coast of West Africa, Congo Basin, lowlands of South-East Asia.
Answer: B.

explanation_steps: The textbook's problems of developed countries: (i) ageing population, (ii) small workforce, (iii) urbanisation problems (pollution, congestion, crime).
Rapid population growth, unemployment and under-utilisation of resources are listed as problems of DEVELOPING countries.
Answer: D.

questions.stem: When two ocean floors collide, one sinks below the other and this forms a:
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'When two ocean floors collide, one sinks below the other and forms a deep trench in the ocean floor'; strong earthquakes and island arcs result.
Ocean–continent collision forms fold mountains (Andes); the San Andreas Fault is a transform (tear) boundary; the East African Rift is a divergent boundary.
Answer: C.
tips: Convergent boundaries: ocean–ocean → trench + island arcs; ocean–continent → trench + fold mountains + volcanoes; continent–continent → high fold mountains (Himalayas).

similar_questions.stem: The Andes were formed when:

questions.stem: Monsoon winds are:

options.B: in summer blowing from land to sea
options.C: the dominant winds on the eastern and western slopes of Eritrea
options.D: in winter blowing from sea to land

explanation_steps: The textbook: monsoons are seasonal winds whose direction reverses between summer and winter; they dominate South, South-East and East Asia.
Summer monsoons blow from sea to land (giving heavy rain); winter monsoons blow from land to sea – so B and D are reversed. C is not stated.
Answer: A.
tips: Summer monsoon: sea → land, wet. Winter monsoon: land → sea, dry.

similar_questions.stem: Which region is most dominated by monsoon winds?
explanation_steps: The textbook: monsoons dominate South, South-East and East Asia (India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka…).

questions.stem: Mr Smith is a geographer who has focused on the Horn of Africa – its location, landforms, climate and political divisions. Collectively his study would be:
explanation_steps: The textbook: regional geography studies a region and all its qualities (physical and human) – e.g. a geographer studying the regional geography of a particular area.
Physical, human and topical/systematic geography study one theme (e.g. climate) across many places.
Mr Smith studies many aspects (physical and political) of one region. Answer: A.
tips: One region, many topics → regional geography. One topic, many regions → topical (systematic) geography.

similar_questions.stem: A geographer who studies climates of the whole world is doing:

questions.stem: World population had slow growth rates up to the industrial revolution of Western Europe. The reasons for that were:

options.A: high infant mortality and short life expectancy
options.B: discovery of vaccinations and public sanitation

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Up to the industrial revolution of western Europe, the world population was few in number and had slow growth rates. This was mainly due to high infant mortality, short life expectancy, periodic famines, and undernourishment.'
Vaccinations and public sanitation came later and REDUCED death rates, causing rapid growth.
Answer: E (A and C).
tips: Before 1750: high birth AND high death rates → slow growth. After the industrial revolution: death rates fell (medicine, sanitation, food) → rapid growth.

similar_questions.stem: Which factor caused rapid population growth after the industrial revolution?
explanation_steps: Improved medical services and sanitation lowered death rates.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Quaternary unconsolidated sediments were deposited along the Red Sea coast when:

options.B: molten materials solidified along the coast
options.C: the climate changed in the Quaternary period
options.D: the sea advanced in the Mesozoic era
options.E: Eritrea fractured in the Eocene epoch

explanation_steps: The textbook: in the Pleistocene epoch of the Quaternary there was an increase of rainfall – the Pluvial Period – which caused heavy erosion on the Highlands; sediments (clay, silt, sand, gravel) were deposited on the coastal areas and, with lacustrine deposits, formed the Quaternary unconsolidated sediments.
The Pluvial Period is a climatic change in the Quaternary. Heavy weathering (A) refers to the Palaeozoic; the Mesozoic sea (D) and Eocene fracturing (E) are older events.
Answer: C.
tips: Pluvial = rainy period in the Pleistocene → erosion in the highlands → deposition on the coast.

similar_questions.stem: The Danakil inland sea dried up and left deposits of potash, gypsum and salt because of:
explanation_steps: The textbook: due to aridity and high temperature the Danakil sea evaporated and dried up.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The major features produced in the lower stage of a river are:

options.A: V-shaped valleys, gorges, interlocking spurs and waterfalls
options.B: Open V-shaped valleys, meanders, river cliffs and ox-bows
options.D: Flood plains, levees, meanders and deltas

explanation_steps: The textbook's lower (old/plain) stage: the river deposits its load – flood plains, levees, meanders and ox-bow lakes, and deltas at the mouth.
A lists upper-stage features; B mostly middle-stage features; C mixes upper-stage features.
Answer: D ('leaves' in the paper is a misprint for 'levees').
tips: Upper = erosion downward (V-valleys, gorges, waterfalls, interlocking spurs). Middle = lateral erosion (meanders, river cliffs). Lower = deposition (flood plains, levees, deltas).

similar_questions.stem: Raised banks of deposited material along the sides of a river in its lower course are called:
explanation_steps: The textbook: a levee is a raised bank formed by deposition when the river floods.
Answer: B.

options.A: According to Malthusian theory, if population growth is not controlled people are trapped in poverty.
options.B: All parts of developed countries enjoy a high standard of living.
options.C: Many people suffer from hunger every year because enough food is not produced in the world.
options.D: The economy of developing countries is based on secondary and tertiary production.
options.E: All third-world countries lack sufficient natural resources.

explanation_steps: The textbook: Malthus 'concluded that if population growth is not controlled, people are trapped in poverty and underdevelopment' (population grows geometrically, food arithmetically).

B is false (textbook: all parts of a developed country may not enjoy a high standard of living), C is false (textbook: enough food is produced every year to feed the entire world population; the problem is distribution, not production), D is false (developing economies are based on primary activities), E is false (many developing countries are rich in resources).

questions.stem: Identify the wrong idea describing lines of latitude and longitude (meridians):

options.A: Latitudes are drawn in an east–west direction.
options.B: Meridians have the same length and narrow towards the top (poles).
options.C: The equator is 0° and a great circle.
options.D: The prime meridian is 0° and all meridians are (halves of) great circles.

A–D are acceptable descriptions (meridians all meet at the poles and each forms half of a great circle). Answer: E.
tips: Latitude: north–south position, lines run east–west, equator 0°. Longitude: east–west position, lines run north–south, prime meridian 0°.

questions.section: Part II – Short answer and completion questions
questions.stem: What are the two types of gradational forces? (2 points)
questions.answer: a) Degradation (denudation) forces – lowering of the land by weathering and erosion. b) Aggradation forces – building up of the land by deposition.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Gradational forces are two types. These are degradation forces and aggradation forces.'
Degradation (denudation) lowers the land by weathering and erosion (sun, rain, wind, rivers, frost, ice). Aggradation builds up low areas by depositing the eroded material.
tips: Gradational forces act from outside (exogenic) and level the surface; tectonic forces act from inside the earth.

similar_questions.stem: Distinguish between degradation and aggradation, giving one landform produced by each.
similar_questions.answer: Degradation lowers the land by weathering and erosion (e.g. a V-shaped valley or a gorge). Aggradation builds up land by deposition (e.g. a flood plain or a delta).
explanation_steps: Degradation = removal.
Aggradation = deposition.

questions.stem: Give any three main causes of soil degradation in Eritrea. (3 points)
questions.answer: Any three of: a) steep slopes; b) deforestation; c) overgrazing. Also acceptable: poor farming practices (e.g. ploughing up and down slopes), frequent droughts, the effects of the long war.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The main causes of soil degradation in Eritrea are the following: (a) steep slopes, (b) deforestation, (c) overgrazing.'

Steep slopes speed up runoff and erosion. Deforestation (for fuel, farmland, construction; worsened by drought and war) removes the protective cover. Overgrazing leaves the ground bare, so rainwater runs off instead of sinking in.
marking_points: Accept drought, war or poor farming methods as alternatives (1 each, max 3)
tips: The three textbook causes are enough for full marks; give a short phrase for each.

similar_questions.stem: Suggest three measures of soil conservation suitable for the Eritrean highlands.
similar_questions.answer: Terracing, afforestation (tree planting), area closures to control grazing, contour ploughing, check dams, crop rotation and manuring.
explanation_steps: Link each measure to a cause: terraces → steep slopes; afforestation → deforestation; area closure → overgrazing.

questions.stem: _________________ is made up of ice crystals formed near the ground when the temperature is below freezing point. (1 point)
explanation_steps: The textbook (forms of condensation): 'Frost is made up of ice crystals formed near the ground when the temperature is below freezing point.'
It forms when the dew point is below 0 °C. Frost can destroy crops.
tips: Dew = water droplets (dew point above 0 °C); frost = ice crystals (dew point below 0 °C).

similar_questions.stem: What is the difference between dew and frost?
similar_questions.answer: Dew is water droplets that condense on cool surfaces when the dew point is above freezing. Frost is ice crystals formed near the ground when the temperature is below freezing point.
explanation_steps: Same process (condensation on a cold surface); the temperature decides the form.

questions.stem: Mention three population problems of developed countries. (3 points)
questions.answer: a) Aging population. b) Small (shortage of) workforce. c) Problems of urbanization – air and water pollution, traffic congestion, noise and crime.
explanation_steps: The textbook, 'Problems of Developed Countries': (i) aging population – a decline in fertility raises the proportion of old people, who depend on the working population;
(ii) small workforce – aging, low birth rates and longer schooling cause a shortage of workers (hence immigration of workers);
(iii) urbanization – environmental damage such as air and water pollution, traffic congestion, noise and crime.
marking_points: Urbanization problems: pollution, congestion, noise or crime (1)
tips: Do not give developing-country problems (rapid growth, unemployment, under-utilisation of resources, uneven distribution).

similar_questions.stem: Mention two population problems of developing countries.
similar_questions.answer: Any two of: rapid population growth, unemployment, under-utilisation of resources, uneven distribution of population.
explanation_steps: These are the textbook's problems of developing countries.

questions.section: Part II – Short answer and completion questions
questions.stem: List any two consequences of global warming. (2 points)
questions.answer: Any two of: a rise in sea level that might flood coastal lands; disruption of agriculture because of frequent droughts; depletion of the ozone layer, leading to diseases. Also acceptable: melting of ice/glaciers, more extreme weather.
explanation_steps: The textbook: the increase of carbon dioxide and other gases in the atmosphere is causing global warming, which has the following consequences:
a rise in sea level that might flood many coastal lands; disruption of agriculture because of frequent droughts; depletion of the ozone layer, which could lead to a number of diseases.
marking_points: 1 point each (max 2): rise in sea level / flooding of coasts; disruption of agriculture (droughts); ozone depletion (diseases); accept melting ice
tips: Write consequences (effects), not causes (burning fuel, deforestation).

similar_questions.stem: What is the main cause of global warming according to the textbook?
similar_questions.answer: The increase of carbon dioxide and other (greenhouse) gases in the atmosphere, mainly from burning fuels and from deforestation.
explanation_steps: Greenhouse gases trap heat → temperature rises.

questions.section: Part II – Short answer and completion questions
questions.stem: Mention any two factors that determine the amount of water in a soil. (2 points)
questions.answer: Any two of: vegetation; climate (amount of rainfall and evaporation); the physical characteristics of the soil (texture, structure and pore spaces).
explanation_steps: The textbook (components of soil): 'Water exists in soil in different quantities, depending on vegetation, climate and the physical characteristics.'
Water enters mainly by infiltration of rainfall; during dry periods the water in the pore spaces is depleted and air fills most of them.
marking_points: 1 point each (max 2): vegetation; climate (rainfall/evaporation); physical characteristics of the soil (texture/pore spaces)
tips: Physical characteristics = texture (sand drains fast, clay holds water), structure, pore spaces.

similar_questions.stem: What are the four main components of soil?
similar_questions.answer: Organic matter (including humus), inorganic (mineral) matter such as clay, silt and sand, air and water.
explanation_steps: Pore spaces hold air and water, on average about half and half.

questions.section: Part II – Short answer and completion questions
questions.stem: Which places are the most important sites of grazing lands in Eritrea? (2 points)
questions.answer: a) Southern Gash-Barka (e.g. Shambiko, Shilalo and Om Hager). b) The Buri Peninsula.
explanation_steps: The textbook (factors of population distribution – grazing lands): 'Southern Gash-Barka, the Buri peninsula and other areas [are] important sites of grazing lands in Eritrea. In the Southern Gash-Barka region, some places like Shambiko, Shilalo and Om Hager are rich in grazing lands.'
tips: The two textbook answers are Southern Gash-Barka and the Buri Peninsula; naming Shambiko, Shilalo or Om Hager also shows Southern Gash-Barka.

similar_questions.stem: Besides grazing lands, name two natural resources that affect population distribution in Eritrea.
similar_questions.answer: Fertile soils/adequate rainfall (e.g. alluvial soils) and fishing grounds (along the coast from Massawa down to Assab).
explanation_steps: Textbook 7.4 lists grazing lands, soil and rainfall, and fishing grounds.

questions.section: Part II – Short answer and completion questions
questions.stem: Which layer of the atmosphere influences the daily activities of human life? (1 point)
explanation_steps: The textbook: the troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere (up to 10–16 km). It contains more than 75 % of the atmosphere, and 'most of the weather changes that influence our daily life take place within this layer'.
tips: Order upward: troposphere → stratosphere → mesosphere → thermosphere (ionosphere) → exosphere.

similar_questions.stem: In which layer of the atmosphere is the ozone layer found?
explanation_steps: Ozone absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays from the sun.

questions.section: Part II – Short answer and completion questions
questions.stem: The Western Lowlands of Eritrea are located in ________________ and ___________________ Zobas (Regions). (2 points)
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The Western Lowlands are found in Zoba Anseba and Zoba Gash-Barka. They extend from the foot of the western slopes to the border with Sudan.'
They include the Barka, Gash and eastern Setit lowlands (500–1000 m a.s.l.).
tips: The Eastern (coastal) lowlands are in the Northern and Southern Red Sea zobas.

similar_questions.stem: In which zobas are the Eastern (coastal) lowlands of Eritrea found?
similar_questions.answer: Northern Red Sea and Southern Red Sea zobas.
explanation_steps: The textbook: the Eastern Lowlands stretch along the Red Sea coast from the border with Djibouti to Ras Kassar (average width 60 km, mostly below 500 m).
The zoba names are general knowledge; the textbook describes only the extent.
